title: Reading Code Is Not Just a Bottleneck
snippet: It was never good at catching bugs. It was how you learned the system
content_html:
Recently I listened to a debate — a senior engineer shared a thought experiment: if your agents ship code 10 times in a row and you have nothing to add each time, is checking the 11th superstitious? If that is the case, reading code has become a bottleneck and a waste of engineers’ precious time.

Huh?

During the same debate another engineer disagreed saying that big labs keep humans on critical paths because they need someone who understands the specific component and architecture when it breaks.

Let’s start from the beginning.

Reading Code Had Two Jobs

Reading code used to serve a dual purpose: 1) catch bugs and 2) help you build a mental map of the solution. Since it was all part of the same process, no one thought of separating the two.

When I made a post about this, one reader replied: “Code review isn’t designed to catch bugs. We’re not compilers. Tests are designed to catch bugs. Code review is designed to ensure our solutions are maintainable”. I mostly agree, and “maintainable” is just another way to describe the second job. Code stays maintainable when someone other than the author understands it well enough to contribute. That understanding is “the map”.

Agents have pulled the two apart. Bug catching can be delegated, but someone still needs to build the map. Review helps build that understanding, but it doesn’t replace what you learn while writing the solution yourself.

Recently, I saw a case where an agent made a change, a human reviewed it, it shipped, and then... production broke. The bug was in how the system handled old records after what they pointed to was gone, and nothing in the code diff gave any clue. I doubt anyone, even a domain expert, would have caught it from the changed lines.

Reading didn’t catch it because the problem lived in a part of the system that a diff doesn’t show.

And it isn’t a one-off: agents write code that looks cool and correct and passes review, and what fails is the hidden connections you can’t see in the changed lines. That’s what the map is for. When you count only the bugs a review catches, you don’t count the understanding that might help you ask the right question next time.

Ten out of ten proves less than it seems

METR did a study on experienced developers working in their own codebases. With AI, they took 19% longer, but they believed AI had made them 20% faster. These were last year’s tools, but the mismatch matters here: the developers thought AI was saving them time when it was costing them time.

Now consider what that earlier thought experiment relied on: “ten times out of ten, I had nothing to add”. That’s self-reporting, and we already have a reason to be suspicious of our own impressions. And there’s no other data: a friend of mine doesn’t even know how many PRs he reviewed last cycle, because review work isn’t tracked anywhere.

Even ten reviews where you had nothing to add only tell you about the setup you used. Change the model or the tools around it, and you’re reviewing a different setup.

The senior engineer who gave the thought experiment also said: “I wrote all the code that runs this company with these two hands, and what I remember about it is laughable next to the model”.

The model may remember more of the code than he does. That doesn’t tell us how much understanding he still brings to a review, or how much a junior would need before trusting the same summary.

A junior who takes this thought experiment as advice skips the struggle that builds that understanding. The senior’s experience doesn’t tell us whether the junior can afford to skip it.

Judgment is built by doing exactly the work we’re now automating away.

Companies hire engineers at mid-level and above, assuming someone else will train the juniors. I wrote about where that ends in I Miss Writing Code: expertise has to come from somewhere.

What can we delegate to agents, and where do we still need to read and write code to build our own understanding?
